challenges.headline: One-off build vs reusable kit
challenges.premise: The request reads as a single-event app: build it, run the event, done.
challenges.alternative: The context flags this as the first recurring trap of event-ops work — many clients running one event today plan to run more, and a reusable event kit needs a different data model (multi-event, configurable zones/categories) from day one.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event-only now and retrofitting multi-event support later means re-architecting the attendee/config model after the fact, likely under the pressure of the next event's own fixed date.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether more events are planned before locking the data model.

challenges.headline: Check-in treated as a boolean
challenges.premise: "Check attendees in" implies one scan per attendee, done or not-done.
challenges.alternative: A second scan can mean a blocked duplicate, an allowed re-entry, or entry into a different zone/session — three different data models, and the context flags this as a near-universal need at real events.
challenges.consequence: A naive one-check-in-per-attendee schema breaks the moment there's a break-out zone, a re-entry after stepping outside, or a multi-session agenda — all common, not exceptional.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to describe the venue layout and re-entry policy before designing the check-in data model.

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed away
challenges.premise: The request describes staff scanning at the entrance with no mention of network conditions.
challenges.alternative: Event venues routinely have dead zones, saturated wifi and shared 4G — offline-first (local snapshot + later sync) is a different architecture than online-only, not a configuration flag.
challenges.consequence: If this is built online-only and the venue's network sags during the pre-keynote rush, the failure is a visible queue at the door in front of the client, with no next sprint to fix it.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm the venue's real connectivity (ideally test on site) and decide offline vs online-only before writing any check-in code.

complexity_reasons: offline-first sync and conflict resolution if connectivity can't be guaranteed
concurrency across multiple entrance devices scanning the same attendee list
throughput target (seconds per attendee) constrains UI, hardware and flow, not just polish
the one-off vs reusable-kit question is undecided and changes the shape of the whole data model
briefs.cost_driver: the offline snapshot/sync and multi-device concurrency layer at the check-in point
risks: The event date can't move — any late-discovered gap (connectivity, duplicate-scan logic, permissions) has no next-sprint fix, only a scramble before doors open.
Attendee list mutability (walk-ins, substitutions, name corrections) isn't addressed; an import-only model will need hand-editing at the door.
GDPR handling of attendee personal data (and any badge photos) isn't addressed at all despite being flagged as a regulatory concern in this domain.
Permissions beyond 'staff' (security overrides, event-manager dashboard) are undefined and are the classic gap that surfaces at acceptance testing.
No rehearsal or device/venue-testing plan exists yet, and this class of app is normally validated on real hardware in the real venue as part of scope.

opportunities.text: Build the offline snapshot + sync engine as a reusable core rather than event-specific glue, since attendee/check-in sync is the hardest part and the client may run more events.
Generalize the check-in engine to handle zone/session-scoped entries from the start, rather than a single entrance-only model.
Standardize the post-event attendance export format so it can serve future events without a rebuild each time.

next_steps: Settle whether this is a one-off build or the first instance of a reusable event kit — this decision reshapes almost everything else and should come first.
Confirm actual venue connectivity and commit to offline-first or online-only architecture before design starts.
Define with the client what a repeat scan means (duplicate, re-entry, different zone) to lock the check-in data model.
Get a concrete throughput target and the device/venue specifics (which phones/tablets, battery, network reach) before estimating the build.

challenges.alternative: Many event-ops clients start with 'just this one event' and then ask for the same app three months later for the next one — at which point a hardcoded, event-specific build has to be rebuilt rather than reconfigured.

challenges.headline: Repeat scan meaning undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats check-in as a single action ('check attendees in') without specifying what a second scan of the same attendee means.
challenges.alternative: A second scan is routinely one of three different things — a blocked duplicate, an allowed re-entry, or a separate zone/session check-in — and each implies a different data model (one check-in record vs. many per attendee).
challenges.consequence: Choosing the wrong model means re-architecting the check-in table and the concurrency logic mid-build, likely discovered only once zones or re-entry come up in testing.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether the event has zones/sessions and what a repeat scan should do before building the check-in data model.
